title: Hagar and the God Who Sees
summary: After ten years in Canaan with no child, Sarai gives her Egyptian slave Hagar to Abram so that she might have a family through her. Hagar conceives, contempt and cruelty follow, and Hagar flees into the desert. There the angel of the LORD finds her, promises her countless descendants and a son named Ishmael, and Hagar names the LORD as the God who sees her.
story: God has just promised Abram a son from his own body and sealed the promise by covenant (Genesis 15). But the promise didn't say through whom, and Sarai is still barren. This chapter is what happens when the promised family tries to secure the promise by its own means. The plan works in the narrow sense, since a son is born, and fails in every other: the household fractures, a vulnerable woman is mistreated, and the son born here will not be the heir of the covenant. Yet the chapter's center is not Abram or Sarai but Hagar, and the surprise is that God meets the one outside the covenant family. Ishmael's line will run alongside Isaac's through the rest of Genesis.
historical:
Abram has now lived ten years in Canaan (verse 3) and is eighty-six at Ishmael's birth (verse 16), eleven years after leaving Harran at seventy-five (Genesis 12:4). Hagar is Egyptian. The text doesn't say how she joined the household, though Genesis 12:16 mentions servants Abram received in Egypt. When she runs, she heads toward Shur, a wilderness region on the route toward Egypt's eastern border, which suggests she was going home. The spring where she stops lies between Kadesh, the oasis region in the far south later known as Kadesh-barnea, and Bered, a place whose location is not known.

Sarai's plan matches recorded practice. The laws of Hammurabi of Babylon (about 1750 BC) address a wife who gives her husband a slave woman to bear children, and they rule that if that slave then claims equality with her mistress, she may be returned to slave status but not sold if she has borne children. An Old Assyrian marriage contract from the nineteenth century BC stipulates that if the wife has not borne a child within two years, she will buy a slave woman for her husband. Such arrangements were legal and socially acceptable; Genesis records them without approving them.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East a woman's standing in her husband's household depended heavily on bearing children, especially sons, and barrenness carried shame as well as grief. A child born to a wife's slave counted legally as the wife's child; Sarai's words, “perhaps I can build a family by her” (verse 2), play on the Hebrew words for son and build. Hagar, meanwhile, had no say at all. She was property, handed from one owner to another, and her body was the means of someone else's plan.

That is why the angel's question in verse 8 matters. Neither Abram nor Sarai ever speaks her name in this chapter; they call her “my maidservant” and “your servant.” The angel of the LORD addresses her as “Hagar, servant of Sarai,” and asks where she has come from and where she is going, as if her own account of her life counts. The wild donkey of verse 12 is the onager, a desert animal admired for its untamed freedom (Job 39:5-8); the image promises that Ishmael will never be anyone's slave.
literary: The chapter is a tight narrative in two scenes, the tent and the desert, bracketed by notes about Sarai's barrenness (verse 1) and Ishmael's birth (verses 15-16). The first scene echoes Genesis 3 closely: Abram “listened to the voice of Sarai” (compare Genesis 3:17), and Sarai “took” Hagar and “gave” her to her husband, the same pair of verbs used when Eve took the fruit and gave it to Adam. The second scene turns on seeing and hearing. Hagar's contempt begins when she sees she is pregnant, and she ends by naming the God who sees her. Her son's name, Ishmael, means God hears, and the angel explains it: “the LORD has heard your cry of affliction.” The verb for Sarai's harsh treatment in verse 6 is the one used for Egypt's oppression of Israel in Genesis 15:13 and Exodus 1:11-12, a bitter irony: here a Hebrew mistress afflicts an Egyptian slave.

outline.t: Sarai's plan and the bitterness that follows
The angel of the LORD finds Hagar in the desert
Hagar names the God who sees her

doctrines.note: God's care extends beyond the covenant line. He finds a runaway slave by a desert spring, knows her name and her story, hears her affliction, and promises her a future. Nothing about Hagar's standing earns this attention; it is simply who God is.

The attempt to hurry God's promise by human means brings envy, blame, and cruelty. Sarai blames Abram, Abram abdicates, and the weakest person in the household suffers most. Genesis tells it plainly and lets the damage speak.

God doesn't remove Hagar's hardship at once; he sends her back with a promise. The chapter offers not an escape but the assurance that suffering is seen and heard by God, who names her son after that fact.

words.note: Anah, to afflict, oppress, or humble. It describes Sarai's harsh treatment of Hagar (verse 6), and the related noun names Hagar's “affliction” (verse 11). The same verb describes Israel's oppression in Egypt, so the reader is meant to feel the reversal: the family of promise does to an Egyptian what Egypt will one day do to them.

Shama, to hear, listen, or obey. It forms Ishmael's name (God hears). The chapter uses it twice with opposite weight: Abram listens to Sarai's plan (verse 2), and the LORD hears Hagar's misery (verse 11).

Ra'ah, to see. Hagar sees that she has conceived and looks down on Sarai, and Sarai's anger follows. At the spring Hagar calls the LORD the God who sees, and the well is named Beer-lahai-roi, usually understood as the well of the Living One who sees me.

christ: Paul uses this story in Galatians 4:21-31, where he says openly that he is reading it figuratively. Hagar, the slave woman whose son was born by human arrangement, stands for the covenant from Mount Sinai and for slavery; Sarah, the free woman whose son came by promise, stands for the Jerusalem above and freedom. His point is that belonging to God rests on promise and the Spirit, not on human effort. Many interpreters in church history, from early Christian writers onward, have also read the angel of the LORD, who speaks with God's own voice, as an appearance of the Son before his incarnation; others see a created messenger bearing God's name and authority. More broadly, the God who seeks out a foreign slave woman whom everyone else overlooked is the same God whom Jesus reveals, who goes looking for the outcast and the lost.

hard.q: Why does the angel send an abused slave back to her mistress?
hard.a:
Verse 9 is hard to read. Hagar has been used, then mistreated, and the angel tells her to “Return to your mistress and submit to her authority.” It's important to see first what the narrative does and doesn't approve. Genesis reports slavery and surrogacy as facts of its world, and it shows the harm this plan causes without pausing to condemn it; description is not endorsement.

Readers then answer the difficulty in different ways. Many point out that a pregnant woman alone in the desert faced likely death, so the command to return preserved her and her son, and it came joined to promises that belonged to her alone, including a son who would never be enslaved. Others stress that the return was temporary: in Genesis 21 Hagar and Ishmael leave for good, again under God's care. Some theologians have made Hagar central to their reflection on survival under oppression; Delores S. Williams's Sisters in the Wilderness (1993) read Hagar's story as a picture of God helping the oppressed to survive and build a life, even where he does not yet bring liberation. The text doesn't resolve every question, but it leaves no doubt about whose side God's attention is on.

questions: Sarai and Abram try to secure God's promise by their own plan. Where are you tempted to force an outcome God has promised or seems slow to give?
No one in the household speaks Hagar's name, but the angel does. Who in your world is spoken about rather than spoken to?
Hagar calls God “the God who sees me.” What difference would it make to believe that God sees you in the place you are most overlooked?
